paragraphs: The absence of a central government will not, then, prove the destruction of the republics of the New World, as has often been claimed. Far from supposing that the American governments are not centralized enough, I shall show later that they are too centralized. The legislative bodies encroach on the authority of the executive every day, and their tendency, like that of the French Convention, is to take it entirely for themselves. In these circumstances the social power is constantly changing hands, because it answers to the power of the people, which in its awareness of its own strength is all too ready to forget the maxims of wisdom and foresight. Here lies its danger. Its vigor, and not its weakness, will probably be the cause of its eventual destruction.

The system of local administration produces several different effects in America. The Americans seem to me to have gone beyond the limits of sound policy in isolating the administration of the government, for order, even in secondary matters, is of national importance. *r Because the State has no administrative officials of its own, stationed at various points across its territory, to whom it can give a common direction, it rarely tries to issue any general police regulations. Europeans often notice the lack of these regulations, and they feel it keenly. The appearance of disorder on the surface leads a European at first to imagine that society is in a state of anarchy, and he does not see his mistake until he has looked deeper into the subject. Certain undertakings matter to the whole State, but they cannot be carried out, because there is no national administration to direct them. Left to the efforts of the towns or counties, under the care of elected or temporary agents, they lead to no result, or at least to no lasting benefit.

r [ The authority that represents the State ought not, I think, to give up the right of inspecting the local administration, even when it does not intervene more actively. Suppose, for instance, that an agent of the government were stationed at some fixed place in the country to prosecute the misdemeanors of the town and county officers. Would not a more uniform order result, without in any way compromising the independence of the township? Nothing of the kind exists in America, however. There is nothing above the county courts, which have, as it were, only an incidental jurisdiction over the offenses they are meant to repress.]

The partisans of centralization in Europe are accustomed to maintain that the government directs the affairs of each locality better than the citizens could do it for themselves. This may be true when the central power is educated and the local districts are ignorant, when it is as quick as they are slow, and when it is used to acting while they are used to obeying. Indeed, it is plain that this double tendency must grow as centralization increases, and that the readiness of the one and the incapacity of the others must become more and more pronounced. But I deny that this is the case when the people is as well-informed, as alert to its interests, and as accustomed to reflect on them as the Americans are. I am convinced, on the contrary, that in this case the collective strength of the citizens will always serve the public welfare more effectively than the authority of the government. It is hard to say with certainty how to rouse a sleeping population and give it passions and knowledge it does not possess. I am well aware that it is a difficult task to persuade men to busy themselves with their own affairs, and it would often be easier to interest them in the fine points of court etiquette than in the repair of their common dwelling. But whenever a central administration claims to replace the people most concerned, I am inclined to suppose that it is either mistaken or trying to mislead. However enlightened and however skillful a central power may be, it cannot by itself take in all the details of the life of a great nation. Such vigilance is beyond human powers. And when it tries to build and set in motion so many complicated springs, it must accept a very imperfect result or wear itself out in futile efforts.

Centralization does succeed more easily in imposing a certain uniformity on the outward actions of men. This uniformity commands our respect for its own sake, whatever it is applied to, like those devotees who worship the statue and forget the deity it represents. Centralization gives an admirable regularity to the routine of business without difficulty. It attends to the details of public order with skill, represses the smallest disorder and the pettiest misdemeanors, and keeps society in a status quo that is safe alike from improvement and from decline. It perpetuates a drowsy precision in the conduct of affairs, which the heads of the administration welcome as a sign of perfect order and public tranquillity. *s In short, it is better at prevention than at action. Its force deserts it when society needs to be disturbed or hurried along in its course, and as soon as the cooperation of private citizens is necessary to carry out its measures, the secret of its weakness is exposed. Even while it asks for their help, it does so on the condition that they act exactly as much as the government chooses, and exactly in the manner it prescribes. They are to take charge of the details without aspiring to guide the system. They are to work in a dark and subordinate sphere, and to judge the acts they have helped to carry out only by their results. These are not the conditions on which the alliance of the human will can be won. Its bearing must be free and its actions responsible, or else (such is the nature of man) the citizen would rather remain a passive spectator than be a dependent actor in schemes he knows nothing about.

s [ China appears to me to offer the most perfect example of the kind of well-being that a completely centralized administration can provide for the nations under it. Travelers assure us that the Chinese have peace without happiness, industry without improvement, stability without strength, and public order without public morality. The condition of society is always tolerable, never excellent. I am convinced that when China is opened to European observation, it will be found to contain the most perfect model of a central administration that exists in the world.]

It cannot be denied that the United States not infrequently feels the lack of those uniform regulations that govern the conduct of every inhabitant of France. Gross cases of social indifference and neglect are to be found, and from time to time disgraceful blemishes appear in complete contrast with the civilization around them. Useful undertakings that cannot succeed without constant attention and rigorous exactness are very often abandoned in the end, for in America, as in other countries, the people is subject to sudden impulses and short bursts of effort. The European is accustomed to finding an official always at hand to interfere in everything he undertakes, and he has some difficulty getting used to the complex machinery of township administration. In general it may be said that the lesser details of police, which make life easy and comfortable, are neglected in America, but that the essential guarantees of man in society are as strong there as anywhere else. In America the power that conducts the government is far less regular, less enlightened, and less learned than in Europe, but a hundred times more authoritative. In no country in the world do the citizens make such efforts for the common good. I know of no people that has established schools as numerous and as effective, places of public worship better suited to the needs of the inhabitants, or roads kept in better repair. Uniformity and continuity of design, the minute arrangement of details, *t and the perfection of an ingenious administration must not be looked for in the United States. But it is easy to find there the signs of a power that, if somewhat rough, is at least robust, and of a life that is full of accidents, but also cheered by activity and effort.

t [ A writer of talent compared the finances of France with those of the United States, and in doing so proved that ingenuity cannot always take the place of a knowledge of facts. He very justly reproaches the Americans for the kind of confusion that exists in the accounts of township expenditure, and after giving the model of a departmental budget in France, he adds:—“We are indebted to centralization, that admirable invention of a great man, for the uniform order and method which prevail alike in all the municipal budgets, from the largest town to the humblest commune.” However much I may admire this result, I see the communes of France, with their excellent system of accounts, sunk in the grossest ignorance of their true interests and abandoned to so incurable an apathy that they seem to vegetate rather than to live. On the other hand, I observe the activity, the information, and the spirit of enterprise that keep society in perpetual labor in those American townships whose budgets are drawn up with little method and still less uniformity. The contrast strikes me, for in my view the purpose of a good government is to ensure the welfare of a people, and not to establish order and regularity in the midst of its misery and distress. I am therefore led to suppose that the prosperity of the American townships and the apparent confusion of their accounts, and the distress of the French communes and the perfection of their budget, may be due to the same cause. At any rate, I am suspicious of a benefit that comes with so many evils, and I do not mind an evil that is made up for by so many benefits.]

Suppose for a moment that the villages and counties of the United States would be governed more usefully by a distant authority they had never seen than by officials drawn from among themselves. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the country would be safer and the resources of society better used if the whole administration were centered in a single hand. Even so, the political advantages the Americans gain from their system would lead me to prefer it to the opposite plan. After all, it does me little good that a vigilant authority protects the tranquillity of my pleasures and constantly keeps every danger from my path, without any care or concern on my part, if this same authority is the absolute master of my liberty and my life. It does me little good if it so monopolizes all the energy of existence that when it languishes everything around it languishes, when it sleeps everything must sleep, and when it dies the state itself must perish.

In certain countries of Europe the natives regard themselves as a kind of settlers, indifferent to the fate of the place where they live. The greatest changes are carried out without their participation and, unless chance happens to inform them, without their knowledge. What is more, the citizen is unconcerned about the condition of his village, the policing of his street, or the repair of the church or the parsonage. He looks on all these things as having nothing to do with himself, and as the property of a powerful stranger whom he calls the government. He has only a life interest in these possessions, and he has no idea of ownership or of improvement. This lack of interest in his own affairs goes so far that if his own safety or that of his children is in danger, he will not try to avert the peril. Instead he will fold his arms and wait for the nation to come to his assistance. This same man, who has so completely given up his own free will, has no natural inclination to obedience. He cowers, it is true, before the pettiest official, but he defies the law with the spirit of a conquered enemy as soon as its superior force is removed. He swings constantly between servitude and license. When a nation has reached this state, it must either change its customs and its laws or perish. The source of public virtue is dry, and though the nation may still contain subjects, the race of citizens is extinct. Such communities are a natural prey to foreign conquest. If they do not disappear from the scene, it is because they are surrounded by other nations similar or inferior to themselves. It is because the instinctive feeling for their country’s claims still lives in their hearts, and because an involuntary pride in its name, or a vague memory of its past glory, is enough to give them the impulse of self-preservation.

Nor can the prodigious efforts that tribes have made in defense of a country that was not their own be cited in favor of such a system. In these cases it will be found that their main motive was religion. The permanence, the glory, or the prosperity of the nation had become part of their faith, and in defending the country they lived in, they defended that Holy City of which they were all citizens. The Turkish tribes never took an active part in the conduct of public affairs, yet they accomplished stupendous enterprises as long as the victories of the Sultan were the triumphs of the Mohammedan faith. In the present age they are in rapid decay, because their religion is departing and only despotism remains. Montesquieu attributed to absolute power an authority peculiar to itself, and in doing so, I think, he gave it an honor it did not deserve, for despotism, taken by itself, can produce no lasting results. On close inspection we shall find that religion, and not fear, has always been the cause of the long-lived prosperity of an absolute government. Whatever efforts may be made, no true power can be founded among men that does not rest on the free union of their inclinations. Patriotism and religion are the only two motives in the world that can permanently direct a whole body politic toward one end.

Laws cannot rekindle the ardor of an extinguished faith, but they can make men take an interest in the fate of their country. Through this influence the vague impulse of patriotism, which never abandons the human heart, may be directed and revived. If it is connected with the thoughts, the passions, and the daily habits of life, it may be consolidated into a lasting and rational feeling.

Let it not be said that the time for the experiment is already past. The old age of nations is not like the old age of men, and every new generation is a new people, ready for the care of the legislator.

It is not the administrative effects but the political effects of the local system that I admire most in America. In the United States the interests of the country are kept in view everywhere. They are an object of concern to the people of the whole Union, and every citizen is as warmly attached to them as if they were his own. He takes pride in the glory of his nation. He boasts of its successes, to which he believes he has contributed, and he rejoices in the general prosperity from which he profits. The feeling he has toward the State is like the one that binds him to his family, and it is through a kind of egotism that he takes an interest in the welfare of his country.

The European generally submits to a public official because the official represents a superior force. To an American, the official represents a right. In America it may be said that no one obeys man, but only justice and the law. If the opinion a citizen holds of himself is exaggerated, it is at least healthy. He confidently trusts in his own powers, which appear to him to be all-sufficient. When a private individual plans an undertaking, however directly it may concern the welfare of society, he never thinks of asking for the cooperation of the government. He publishes his plan, offers to carry it out himself, seeks the help of other individuals, and struggles manfully against all obstacles. No doubt he is often less successful than the State would have been in his place, but in the end the sum of these private undertakings far exceeds anything the government could have done.

Because the administrative authority is within the reach of the citizens, whom it in some degree represents, it arouses neither their jealousy nor their hatred. Because its resources are limited, everyone feels that he must not rely on its assistance alone. Thus, when the administration sees fit to intervene, it is not left to itself as it is in Europe. The duties of private citizens are not supposed to have lapsed because the State helps in carrying them out. On the contrary, everyone is ready to guide and support it. This combination of individual efforts with those of the public authorities often accomplishes what the most energetic central administration would be unable to do. It would be easy to cite several facts in proof of what I say, but I prefer to give only one, with which I am better acquainted. *u In America the means that the authorities have for discovering crimes and arresting criminals are few. There is no State police, and passports are unknown. The criminal police of the United States cannot be compared to that of France. The magistrates and public prosecutors are not numerous, and the examinations of prisoners are quick and oral. Nevertheless, in no country does crime more rarely escape punishment. The reason is that everyone considers himself concerned in providing evidence of the act committed and in stopping the offender. During my stay in the United States I saw committees form spontaneously to pursue and prosecute a man who had committed a great crime in a certain county. In Europe a criminal is an unhappy being struggling for his life against the ministers of justice, while the population merely watches the conflict. In America he is looked on as an enemy of the human race, and the whole of mankind is against him.
u [ See Appendix, I.]

I believe that provincial institutions are useful to all nations, but nowhere do they seem to me more indispensable than among a democratic people. In an aristocracy order can always be maintained in the midst of liberty, and because the rulers have a great deal to lose, order is a first-rate concern to them. In the same way, an aristocracy protects the people from the excesses of despotism, because it always possesses an organized power ready to resist a despot. But a democracy without provincial institutions has no security against these evils. How can a populace unaccustomed to freedom in small matters learn to use it with moderation in great affairs? What resistance can be offered to tyranny in a country where every private individual is powerless, and where the citizens are united by no common tie? Those who dread the license of the mob, and those who fear the rule of absolute power, ought equally to desire the gradual growth of provincial liberties.

On the other hand, I am convinced that democratic nations are the most exposed to falling under the yoke of a central administration, for several reasons, among them the following. The constant tendency of these nations is to concentrate all the strength of the government in the hands of the only power that directly represents the people, because beyond the people nothing can be seen but a mass of equal individuals merged together. But when that same power already holds all the attributes of government, it can hardly refrain from reaching into the details of administration, and an opportunity to do so is sure to present itself in the end, as happened in France. In the French Revolution there were two impulses in opposite directions, which must never be confused. One favored liberty, the other despotism. Under the ancient monarchy the King was the sole author of the laws, and beneath the sovereign’s power certain half-destroyed vestiges of provincial institutions could still be made out. These provincial institutions were incoherent, loosely constructed, and often absurd. In the hands of the aristocracy they had sometimes been turned into instruments of oppression. The Revolution declared itself the enemy of royalty and of provincial institutions at the same time. It lumped together everything that had come before it, despotic power and the checks on its abuses alike, in indiscriminate hatred, and its tendency was both to overthrow and to centralize. This double character of the French Revolution is a fact that the friends of absolute power have skillfully exploited. Can they be accused of working for despotism when they defend that central administration, which was one of the great innovations of the Revolution? *v In this way popularity may be won along with hostility to the rights of the people, and the secret slave of tyranny may be the professed admirer of freedom.
v [ See Appendix K.]

I have visited the two nations in which the system of provincial liberty has been most perfectly established, and I have listened to the opinions of different parties in those countries. In America I met men who secretly aspired to destroy the democratic institutions of the Union. In England I found others who openly attacked the aristocracy. But I know of no one in either country who does not regard provincial independence as a great benefit. In both countries I have heard a thousand different causes given for the evils of the State, but the local system was never mentioned among them. I have heard citizens attribute the power and prosperity of their country to a multitude of reasons, but they all placed the advantages of local institutions in the foremost rank. Am I to suppose that when men who are so naturally divided in their religious opinions and political theories agree on one point (and one they experience every day), they are all in error? The only nations that deny the usefulness of provincial liberties are those that have the fewest of them. In other words, those who are unacquainted with the institution are the only people who condemn it.
